item.title: Republicans face a fight for control of Congress as midterm elections get underway
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It's Election Day in America, with voters heading to the polls to determine control of the U.S. House and Senate for the next two years. Republicans are defending their slim congressional majorities, but President Donald Trump predicts the GOP will hold the House and Senate for the final two years of his presidency. "We're going to win and let's make the next two years bigger and better and stronger than ever before," Trump told supporters Sunday night at a rally in Kansas. But Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings. Democracy 2026: Stay Up To Date With The Fox News Election Hub President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally at the Salina Regional Airport, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Salina, Kansas. The GOP is also facing a potential turnout deficit, with public opinion polls indicating Democrats are more energized than Republicans to cast ballots in the midterms. Read On The Fox News App Early voting in the midterms has shattered previous records, with more than 54 million people already casting ballots, according to The Associated Press. That's nearly 9 million more ballots cast in early voting than in 2022, the previous midterm elections. With early voting traditionally favoring Democrats, Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, pointing to Election Day turnout, recently told Fox News Digital, "If our voters turn out, we win." Sign Up To Get The Politics Newsletter A voter fills out their ballot at a polling location inside Wayne Community College Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. The political climate has the GOP playing plenty of defense on the campaign trail, as the president tries to energize the GOP base. Trump's event in red-leaning Kansas, which he touted as his 30th rally over the past month, came hours after the Fox News Power Rankings shifted the state's Senate race from Lean Republican to Toss-up. Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, who is challenging GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, is aiming to become the first Democrat in nearly a century to win a Senate election in Kansas. The Fox News Power Rankings, as well as many of the leading nonpartisan political handicappers, point to Democrats retaking control of the House, with the majority in the Senate a toss-up heading into Election Day. "Think of what is possible tomorrow: Democrats can flip the House, take back the Senate, and stop Trump’s harmful agenda," Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin spotlighted in an Election Eve social media post. Also up for grabs in this year's elections — governorships in 36 of the 50 states. Plus, all but four states are holding legislative elections. And voters will also weigh in on 145 statewide ballot measures in states from coast to coast. The big question with Election Day upon us — have the public opinion polls that point to a potential blue wave undercounted Republican voters? Leavitt Says Trump Defying Midterm Headwinds As He Barnstorms Country The Election Day sign outside town hall in Newfields, New Hampshire, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. We'll find out in the coming hours. Until then, here's a closer look at what's up for grabs on Election Day 2026. Republicans currently control the chamber 53-47, which means Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority. The GOP needs to hold at least 50 seats to retain control of the chamber, since Republican Vice President JD Vance is the tie-breaking vote in the Senate. Besides Kansas, Republicans are also playing defense in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, which are all rated toss-ups in the Power Rankings. They're also defending seats in competitive races in Kansas, which is rated Lean Republican, and Ohio, which is rated Lean Democrat. Democrats are on defense in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire. The GOP is hanging on to a razor-thin majority in the House, with Democrats needing a net gain of just three seats to reach 218, which would hand them the majority. A good night for the Democrats could see them ending up with as many as 240 seats in the 435-seat chamber, according to the Power Rankings. But if Republicans have a good night, they could end up with 212 seats. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party. The earliest-closing district polls on election night will give some sense of the House’s future. "Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle," Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings, said. There are currently 26 Republican and 24 Democratic governors. The Power Rankings list three states where the GOP controls the governor's office – Alaska, Nevada and Georgia – as toss-ups. Wisconsin, which has an open Democratic-controlled governor's office, is also rated a toss-up. The gubernatorial races in red states Florida, Kansas and Texas are rated Lean Republican, according to the Power Rankings. Meanwhile, the showdowns in Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio and Oregon are rated Lean Democrat. Referendums requiring voters to present identification when they show up at the polls, or bans on noncitizen voting, are on the ballot in 11 states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Kansas, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, South Dakota and West Virginia. Voters in Alaska will also decide if they want to repeal the state’s ranked choice voting system, open primaries and a campaign finance disclosure rule. Voters approved the current system in 2020 and narrowly kept it in 2024. But the voting system has come under fresh scrutiny amid the controversy over a potential spoiler candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race. Voters in Virginia will decide whether the right to vote should be restored to convicted felons upon their release. Roughly a dozen states are holding ballot measures on Election Day that are related to voting. California's Proposition 40 is making national headlines. The measure, the first of its kind, would slap a one-time 5% tax on wealth for Californians worth over $1 billion, with the vast majority of the revenue generated going to pay for healthcare. Also in the spotlight is a millionaires' tax in Washington state. If passed, the referendum would repeal a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million a year, which state lawmakers recently approved. Washington state currently does not have a personal income tax. Voters in Maryland, Missouri and Colorado weigh in on ballot measures on congressional redistricting, as the mid-decade redistricting fight between Democrats and Republicans will be waged again in 2028. Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state have referendums on transgender students’ participation in sports. Colorado also has a referendum on blocking gender transition surgeries for minors and preventing state or federal funding from being used for those operations. Voters in Missouri weigh in on repealing a right to abortion and banning gender transition medical care for children. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions. California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development. The first poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET, with the final poll closings happening at 1 a.m. ET. 6 p.m. ET: Polls close in parts of Kentucky and Indiana. 7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. The final polls in Kentucky and Indiana close. And most polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. 7:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia. 8 p.m. ET: Polls close in Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, D.C. The remaining polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. Most polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota. 8:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arkansas. 9 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. The final polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota. 10 p.m. ET: Polls close in Montana and Utah. Most polls also close in Idaho and Oregon. Click Here To Download The Fox News App 11 p.m. ET: Polls close in California and Washington state, with the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon also closing. Midnight ET: Polls in all of Hawaii and most of Alaska close, with the remaining polls in Alaska closing at 1 a.m. ET. Original article source: The battle for Congress is just the beginning. item.title: Trump says U.S. will halt $4 billion in annual aid to Israel and shift to selling arms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday. The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years. Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel . Even far-right conservatives, who have supported Trump in the past, have taken issue with U.S. support for Israel, with prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson openly questioning the value of the relationship. “You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.” There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu’s office. But at least some of his political opponents were cautious. Yair Golan, a leader in Israel’s opposition bloc, said an end to U.S. military aid would deal a “severe blow to Israel’s security” at a time when the country is fighting wars on multiple fronts. “The burden of funding defense needs at such a critical juncture will fall entirely upon the Israeli public,” Golan, a former deputy military chief, said in a statement. Tens of billions of dollars have gone to Israel The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years. In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries. Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point. He told The Economist in January that he wanted to “taper off” U.S. military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was “in the works.” Trump says critics can easily target the $4 billion payment But the optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point. “The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” Trump said Tuesday on Fox. “And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.” Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years. There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the U.S. has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance. In addition, much of the assistance the U.S. provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the U.S. economy. Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, U.S. defense contractors may see an impact. There was more aid after the Gaza war started An academic study published last year showed the U.S. under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict . Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the U.S. had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years. While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of U.S. military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-says-us-halt-4-140212112.html

item.title: U.S. intelligence sharing has fractured under Trump, officials say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Erin Banco and Jonathan Landay WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - US intelligence sharing on Iran and other global threats with Congress and across the federal government has slowed and, in some cases, temporarily stopped during President Donald Trump's second term, according to eight current and former officials and people briefed on the matter. Former officials and outside experts said the disruptions risk leaving policymakers with an incomplete picture of threats facing ‌the country, echoing intelligence failures exposed after the Sept. 11, 2001, al Qaeda attacks. The slowdown comes as the administration weighs whether to resume strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Tuesday. The problems emerged during ‌Tulsi Gabbard's tenure as director of national intelligence, amid deep tensions between her office and the CIA. While those tensions have subsided since her resignation in June, problems stemming from the clash persist, according to two US officials familiar with the matter. The CIA has stopped co-authoring assessments with the National Intelligence Council (NIC), ​an analytical group within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the officials said, reducing the number of reports that pull together the intelligence community's views for decision-makers on subjects including Iran. Lawmakers and their staffs also briefly stopped receiving intelligence reports from Gabbard's office in the days after the US military intervention in Iran in June 2025 and again after the capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, according to two people familiar with the matter. Gabbard's team had accused lawmakers of leaking to the press. The disruption in intelligence sharing has not been previously reported. CIA spokesperson Liz Lyons said the CIA "participates fully" in the process of providing intelligence assessments through the Presidential Daily Brief, which is led by ODNI, and through the NIC. Now, some former officials are working on a ‌bipartisan basis at Stanford University's Hoover Institution to draw up plans to rebuild the intelligence ⁠community in the next administration, four former US officials said. “All of these things are adding up in a really complex world where policymakers need to have a more sophisticated, nuanced, and integrated view of the world, and they are getting less,” said Beth Sanner, a former deputy director of national intelligence during Trump's first term. TURF WARS AND REDUCED COOPERATION The problems inside the intelligence community ⁠started last year amid significant cuts to national security agencies, including the ODNI and the CIA, as Trump moved to remove or sideline officials he viewed as disloyal. Some analysts who remain at the intelligence agencies are now careful to not write assessments at odds with White House’s views for fear of political retaliation, two former officials and a current US official said. The officials did not say which topics the analysts were avoiding. “Analysts still do the work, but this White House has made them irrelevant because the president treats unwelcome information as disloyalty,” said Julia Curlee, ​a ​former CIA analyst who said she was fired from the Trump National Security Council last year for being transgender. The White House did not ​respond to a request for comment. The situation was worsened by what officials described as one of ‌the biggest turf wars in three decades between two of the most important agencies: the CIA and the ODNI, which was formed in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 attacks. Reuters earlier detailed the dispute between the agencies. The infighting between the agencies — triggered when Gabbard's office revoked the security clearances of current and former intelligence officials a year ago — reached the point where White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles had to intervene several times to defuse tensions, three former officials said. The National Intelligence Council, which for decades has been a key resource for officials and lawmakers making foreign policy decisions, lost its main author when the CIA stopped writing into the assessments last year. The assessments are meant to consolidate the views of the nation’s 18 intelligence agencies, and the council relied heavily on the CIA for analysis on topics like Iran and Russia. While the CIA continued sharing intelligence with the NIC and working with it on some reports, its analysts focused on their own assessments. Since the move, the intelligence council, which was also ‌hit by staff cuts, has slowed production of its assessments, two people familiar with the matter said. None have focused on the war in ​Iran, five current and former officials said. In response to a request for comment, an ODNI official said the group has maintained assessment levels close to "historic ​trendlines." "While Tulsi did not utilize the NIC, DNI Clayton has proven to be a good steward of the ​IC and recognizes the value of the NIC," said a US official, referring to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. NEW BARRIERS Some former intelligence officials worry that new barriers are appearing between agencies. "The problem ‌is that by taking actions which have the effect of hollowing out institutions where there's ​actual intelligence community coordination on things, you're creating little lily pads, ​and then everybody can pick their own lily pad to listen to,” said Morgan Muir, the former deputy director of national intelligence in the Biden administration who also briefed President George W. Bush. Gabbard's office also stopped briefing Congress on election threats in 2025, according to two people familiar with the matter and a former US official. Clayton, who became director of national intelligence in August, has resumed congressional briefings on election threats, officials said. "Director Clayton remains committed ​to ensuring that ODNI and the intelligence community have the resources they need to continue ‌informing key U.S. government decision-makers and keeping Americans safe," ODNI said in a statement to Reuters. In another clash between agencies, the FBI late last year stopped sharing some intelligence with the National Counterterrorism Center for several ​weeks after the center's then-head, Joe Kent, and his staff tried to investigate the shooting of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, two former officials said. FBI leaders told Kent they believed NCTC was overstepping ​its authority. The FBI did not respond to a request for comment. (Reporting by Erin Banco; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/exclusive-us-intelligence-sharing-fractured-110514786.html

item.title: Trump put himself on the midterms ballot without running. Now his legacy is at stake.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump’s political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office. Trump has crisscrossed the country, holding 28 in-person campaign rallies in addition to a series of tele-rallies. The president has made stops in Republican strongholds like Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and even Alaska in an effort to keep the states firmly in the red column. He’s also visited a number of deep-red states like Mississippi and South Carolina, where polls show closer than expected races. While Trump has argued his rallies have boosted Republican incumbents and candidates in the states, recent polling suggests otherwise. A New York Times/Siena poll released the day before Election Day showed Democrats with leads in Senate races in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska. Trump’s heavy political investment in the states means he could end up shouldering the blame for a potential blue wave, which could impact the GOP beyond Election Day. Republicans warn that a blue wave would be detrimental to the last two years of the Trump administration, and by extension, his legacy. “It impacts his ability to drive policy over the next two years, or if a Supreme Court nomination comes up, or fill in the blank in terms of even Cabinet turnover,” said one Republican strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity. “All of that too will help shape his legacy, and it’s how people remember you at the end that guides you into the history books.” In a statement to The Hill on Monday, the Republican National Committee (RNC) warned that Democrats would “obstruct” Trump’s agenda and that their “disastrous economic policies” would drive jobs overseas. “The president knows what’s at stake this cycle, which is why he’s barnstormed the country to encourage our voters to support Republican candidates that will advance his agenda and deliver for the American people,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. But during an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump did not appear entirely focused on the elections that could impact the trajectory of his last two years in office. The president spent the first 22 minutes of his 37-minute address — largely viewed as a closing message before the midterms — talking about his administration’s efforts to repair the Reflecting Pool. Trump showed off a number of pre-renovation pictures of the pool and at one point invited Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to the podium to give brief remarks. Trump also touted his numerous beautification projects and lower crime in the nation’s capital. Republican operative Rob Stutzman called Trump’s speech “another Captain Queeg moment,” a reference to a character from Herman Wouk’s 1951 novel “The Caine Mutiny” who is considered an unstable and incompetent commander. A second Republican strategist said, “What the utter f--- was that?” when asked for their reaction to Trump’s speech at the Reflecting Pool. “Republicans were hoping that he would have some sort of a closing message, some sort of American message with it, with a wonderful backdrop that could maybe be of help in the closing hours here,” the unnamed GOP strategist said. “As we Republicans are losing touch with the public, it looked like he was losing touch with reality.” One national Republican operative noted the speech was “not surprising” considering Trump’s communication style but expressed frustration with the closing message. “This perfectly encapsulates his messaging throughout this entire campaign cycle, but it’s deeply frustrating when we need to be laser-focused on turning out our low propensity voters tomorrow,” the operative said. A third Republican strategist defended the speech, arguing the Reflecting Pool was “a hook” for Trump to be able to talk about issues like crime and immigration. “It’s one of these things that wherever you get the opportunity to speak to a national audience, you’re going to talk about the midterms even if you have to start with something else,” the strategist said. Trump did take some time during his speech Monday to urge Republicans to turn out on Election Day. “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” the president said. “Now, that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is — Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad president — for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms.” “We gave this a very strong shot,” he added. Much of the GOP’s strategy has hinged on turning out its low-propensity base as much as possible, arguably a tall order for any political party in a nonpresidential election. Republicans hoped to defy that trend by dispatching Trump on the campaign trail, urging voters to “pretend” like he is on the ballot. “The amount of rallies he did shows he ‘believes’ that he’s on the ballot tomorrow,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. “He worked hard, and he’s right: Tomorrow’s outcome is a reflection on him.” In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to Trump as the GOP’s “best messenger” and “unmatched motivator” who is “committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” But some Republicans are unsure whether that tactic will ultimately work. “So far from what we’ve seen, those rallies have not done what they were meant to do,” said the first unnamed Republican strategist. Democrats have been heartened by signs of early turnout in key battlegrounds, but Republicans argue that a large share of their voters tend to vote in person on Election Day. “They’re banking on these Republicans and the folks that he’s trying to rally to show up tomorrow, and Republicans historically and should do exceedingly well tomorrow,” the first Republican strategist said. “But the fact is, they still underperformed in places like Texas and in Florida in the early vote.” According to data released by Texas’s secretary of State, 7.7 million voters in the Lone Star State voted early. Meanwhile in Florida, registered Republicans led registered Democrats in early voting by just a little more than 200,000 voters. By comparison, in 2022, registered Republicans led Democrats in early voting by just a little less than 500,000 voters. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Sunday sounded the alarm over low turnout in the state, which has become known as a nerve center for Republican politics. “If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you’re going to be wondering what happened. That’s just the reality,” DeSantis said at a campaign event. “The reality is gas is higher, and that’s not good. Some of these Republicans act like it’s no big deal. I disagree with that. It is a big deal to people,” the Florida governor continued. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to The Hill. item.title: Early voting has broken records, but the numbers tell a complicated story
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
On the eve of Election Day a record number of Americans have already passed judgement on President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress. Roughly 54 million voters cast their early ballots over this past weekend ahead of the Nov. 3 election, according to the University of Florida Election Lab . The deluge offers a glimpse into a forecasted wave election that many experts believe could sweep Democrats in power for the president's final two years in the White House. Every state has different rules on compiling voters' age, race or party affiliation with some providing no demographic statistics at all. But it does reveal important voter behavior and some demographics that paint a clearer picture about who is more motivated in the 2026 midterms. Michael McDonald, a political science professor who runs the Election Lab, said the initial outlook indicates a younger, more diverse and politically independent electorate is showing up. "I can confidently say that the 2026 election will be the most diverse midterm electorate in U.S. history," in an Oct. 28 post on X. But the data alone, much like the various polls , cannot predict the outcome of who will be in charge of the House and Senate next year, McDonald and others have warned. Here's a look at the big takeaways from the early voting totals. A lot more people are showing up than in 2022 For starters, 8 million more people took advantage of the early in-person and mail-in ballot options over the weekend than during the last 2022 midterms, which gave Republicans control of the House during former President Joe Biden 's term. Political observers are marveling at those numbers and note how they surged in places with more competitive Senate contests, such as Ohio, Maine and Michigan. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton have locked horns in arguably the most watched race of this year's cycle. The early totals show more than 7.7 million people have cast early ballots, which surpasses the Lone Star State's high mark of 40% turnout during the 2018 midterms. "Their record for a midterm election is 8.3 million total. So they're just over about 600,000 or so ballots away from their highest turnout ever... Election Day hasn't even happened yet. That's remarkable," David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said during CBS' Face the Nation on Nov. 1. Same goes for Georgia, where more than 2.8 million voters have showed up already representing a 13% increase compared to 2022; Michigan with more than 2.3 million marking a 26% increase; and South Carolina where about 1.1 million have shown up compared to approximately 620,000 four years ago which is a whomping 75% increase. Records were also broken in North Carolina, where Democrats are hoping former Gov. Roy Cooper can flip a GOP-held Senate seat against former RNC Chair Michael Whatley. The Tar Heel State began sending out early voting mail-in ballots Oct. 15 and combined with in-person about 2.8 million have reportedly showed up already. That is a 31% increase compared to the midterm election four years ago, Western Carolina University political scientist Chris Cooper said in an Oct. 31 post on Substack . "Voter turnout was higher on every day of early voting than on the comparable day in 2022," he said. 'Bloodbath': Democrats, independents turnout is up while GOP is down Far more Democrats than Republicans made their voices heard in the early voting process with some states outpacing their 2024 presidential totals, the preliminary data show. Of the 54 million ballots cast, about 43% were from Democrats and 32% were from GOP voters, with the about 25% coming from independent or "unaffiliated" voters. Keep in mind that these statistics are limited to the 27 states that report party affiliation. It also reflects the voter's registration rather than their exact choice on the ballot. But some Republicans are already expressing nervousness about the low GOP turnout , especially given Trump's unpopularity among those showing up more. An AP-NORC poll released Oct. 8, for example, found 25% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the economy, with just 9% of Democrats and 23% of independents agreeing. "I am deeply, deeply worried. What we're seeing across the country is massive Democrat turnout," Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, during an Oct. 30 episode of "The Verdict," his podcast. "Democrats are showing up. They are energized. They hate, hate, hate Donald Trump. If the election were over today, if just the early votes that have been cast so far were counted, Republicans would lose massively. It would not be close. We would lose both the House and Senate. It would be a bloodbath." For the past several weeks Trump and his allies have been zig-zagging across the nation, focusing heavily on conservative strongholds in order to motivate their base. He is set to speak at the Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., capping off a blitz of last-minute appearances in states where Republicans face competitive challengers. GOP voters historically have swarmed Election Day when tens of millions of Americans will likely to flock the polls as well, but experts say the early voting patterns mirror past trends. "It would be highly unusual for Election Day to be dramatically different than in the past, so I would not hold out hope for a huge Republican wave to make up for their in-person early voting deficit where we are seeing a lack of Republican early voting engagement," McDonald said on his Substack. Racially diverse and younger voters fueling turnout The United States is becoming a more racially and ethnically diverse nation, and that's showing up in our elections as a higher percentage of Black and Hispanic voters make up the electorate. Of the handful of states that submit race and ethnicity information from early voting totals there is a noteworthy uptick among voters of color, while voting among White people lags behind and remains similar to 2022 levels. Hispanic turnout in Texas is especially noteworthy given it has exceeded the 2024 presidential levels , fueled largely by younger voters, Tom Bonier, a Democratic data and polling expert, told USA TODAY in an October interview. In the state's predominantly Hispanic counties, analysts say they are finding turnout to be higher than the statewide average. Trump and the GOP will need to hold their gains among Hispanic voters , who helped fuel his 2024 victory but has soured on the administration especially over its strict immigration enforcement campaign. The Pew Research Center found Trump's approval among Hispanic voters sits at 24% , which is down from 38% in February 2025. Among Black voters, who make up a larger share of the South electorate, there is reported anger of Trump's redistricting war that carved up many majority-Black congressional districts. That is could help to fuel a surge being seen in southern states such as Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina, where there's a Senate race surprisingly within the margin of error . The Election Lab shows Black early voting accounts for about 32% of Georgia's turnout thus far, which is about three percentage points better than during the 2022 midterm. Even that small jump, however, can be significant given the Peach State's toss-up status, particularly in its closely watched race for governor between Democrat Keisha Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, and Republican Keith Jackson, a healthcare CEO. In South Carolina, for instance, the numbers show Black voters making up about 27% of the electorate which is significantly higher than in past cycles overall. McDonald said by all indicators this midterm should be a good one for Democrats and that figures coming from these states show elevated engagement from those demographics. "Since the Democratic coalition is more diverse, their higher engagement levels will yield a more diverse electorate," he said. item.title: NASA administrator defends 20-year-old Learjet co-pilot after Florida crash
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman took to his personal social media account Nov. 2 to defend the female co-pilot of the Learjet that crashed near Palm Beach, Florida. The private jet, bound from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, plummeted into the ground Nov. 1 near Greenacres and exploded into a fireball. All nine people onboard were killed. The cause of the crash was not immediately known, but heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time the jet went down, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement. Moments before the crash, a person in the cockpit said the crew was "managing the ice," encountering "moderate" turbulence and seeking "better rides," according to audio posted by LiveATC, a website that broadcasts air traffic control communications. That dramatic audio led to significant online criticism of the 20-year-old co-pilot, Nathalia Filgueiras, from Boca Raton. The pilot has not been identified. “Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts,” Isaacman wrote on X. “Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories. God bless them and their loved ones.” Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from… — Jared Isaacman (@rookisaacman) November 2, 2026 NASA Administrator defends Learjet copilot “Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile strikes to DEI to critiquing this poor woman’s final radio calls,” Isaacman wrote. Isaacman is an experienced jet pilot and commercial astronaut. He bankrolled and organized two orbital spaceflights with SpaceX. Both included women onboard, and his first, Inspiration4, featured a female pilot , Sian Proctor. The NASA administrator went on to state that Filgueiras remained professional throughout the situation, knowing her life was about to end. She communicated with air traffic control right up until the crash. "She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," he wrote. “I understand the public interest given the footage and audio. But you do not know the aircraft’s maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit,” Isaacman wrote. The leaked cockpit communication with air traffic control revealed that the crew saw ice and experienced turbulence before the crash occurred. Isaacman said that it is common for charter companies, which fly these small jets, to hire fairly new commercial pilots and enable them to gain experience before many become commercial pilots. Filgueiras would have likely had all the applicable training, requirements, and checkouts required from the Federal Aviation Administration, he wrote. Evidence suggests the aircraft began breaking apart before impact, National Transportation Safety Board member Thomas Chapman said at a Monday news conference. Brooke Edwards is a Space Reporter for Florida Today. Contact her at bedwards@floridatoday.com or on X: @brookeofstars . item.title: Ballot counting issues reported in key New York swing district
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Election Day is here. Today, voters across the United States are heading to the polls to cast their ballots in the 2026 midterms . And with control of Congress up for grabs, the stakes are high for both parties as President Trump heads into his final two years in office. Democrats are seeking to regain control of both the House and Senate, while Republicans, who have held narrow majorities in both chambers since January 2025, are seeking to retain control. In the House, there are 435 seats. And while all of them are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% (or about 350 seats) are not considered competitive. The GOP currently holds 218 seats, compared with 214 held by Democrats. One seat is occupied by an independent (Rep. Kevin Kiley of California), and there are two vacancies (seats formerly held by GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas and Democratic Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick of Florida, who each resigned). To retake control of the House , Democrats would need a net gain of four seats. In the Senate, there are 100 seats, with 35 up for grabs and 12-or-so considered competitive . Republicans currently hold 53 seats compared with 45 held by Democrats. There are two independents — Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine — who caucus with the Democrats. To wrest back control of the Senate, Democrats would need a net gain of four seats. To maintain Senate control, Republicans could still lose a net of three seats, since a 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote. There are also 36 gubernatorial races and numerous ballot measures to keep an eye on. Trump, whose approval ratings are at or near all-time lows, has spent the last month campaigning in battleground states, urging voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot to encourage higher turnout in hopes that it'll help Republicans avert a so-called blue wave . Some members of the GOP, however, appear to be bracing for one. "It could be quite a brutal evening," one senior GOP official told Politico . "Once the dominoes start falling, it becomes hard to stop them." item.title: Passengers in Florida crash identified as family of 4, their caretaker and another couple
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The pilot of the Bahamas-bound Learjet that crashed in Palm Beach County, Fla., on Nov. 1 has been identified . According to FAA records and his former employer, Jeff Gregory, 55, of Gilbertsville, Penn., was piloting the plane that crashed, killing all nine people aboard, including his copilot, Nathalia Filgueiras , and seven passengers, Fox 29 reports . The families of Filgueiras and the passengers had previously confirmed their deaths. Camila Corteleti identified her 20-year-old daughter as one of the pilots of the private jet, the New York Times reported. A joint statement from the families was released on social media. "With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1," the statement said. A tribute to Sharp and her family was posted on her Instagram page , saying, "On behalf of friends and family, it is with a heavy heart that we share that our dearest Helen was taken from us too soon. If you knew Helen, you knew how full of life she was. She simply radiated." Authorities had still not publicly confirmed the identities of those on board the plane at a news conference on Nov. 2, during which they said weather conditions were a major factor in the federal investigation into the fatal crash. The National Transportation Safety Board told reporters on Nov. 2 that ice was forming on the jet as it experienced moderate turbulence. Miami air traffic control granted the pilot permission to climb from 35,000 feet to 37,000 feet to avoid precipitation, but shortly afterward, an emergency was declared with a mayday call. Air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC captured the crew's comments leading up to the crash. Someone in the cockpit can be heard saying "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, Reuters reported. "We're going to crash into the ground," the person said. The Learjet 60, which had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, went down at about 12:50 p.m. ET near Cresthaven, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The NTSB said all nine people on board were killed, including two crew members and seven passengers. The NTSB said it's unclear if Filgueiras was at the controls at the time of the crash. A man who was leaving the area of the crash sustained a leg injury, officials said. Dashcam footage posted to social media by an eyewitness showed the aircraft falling toward the ground beside a road and exploding into a fireball, narrowly missing cars and homes. The impact left a "massive crater" near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a news conference. About 600 residents were evacuated to two shelters, he said. People stand near a crater formed after the Learjet 60 crashed. Vanessa Lara/via REUTERS "We have a lot of work to do on scene — this will be a several-day process," NTSB senior investigator Timothy Monville said during Nov. 2's news conference. "The biggest obstacle we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway." Investigations are also hampered because the crash-site crater is partially filled with water. The NTSB said it will interview witnesses to the accident as part of its investigation and encouraged anyone with relevant information, videos or audio to contact the NTSB by email at witness@ntsb.gov. Some evidence indicates that parts of the plane broke off before the private jet crashed, according to NTSB member Tom Chapman. "I want to note that if any members of the community find debris, please do not move it," he said. "Contact us or local authorities, and we will respond appropriately." He also told reporters that, according to records, a cockpit voice recorder was installed, but the NTSB doesn't know whether it was still on board. "Sometimes these things change over time," Chapman said. "Of course we're very hopeful that we can recover it. Too early to know, but that will be very important data." What we know about the victims Among the victims was the private jet's pilot, Gregory. His former employer, East Coast Jets, a private jet company in Allentown where he worked in 2016 and 2017, said he was an aviator with years of experience , according to the New York Times. "We are deeply saddened to learn that Captain Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach," a spokesperson for East Coast Jets said in a statement on Nov. 2. His copilot Filgueiras's mother said she earned her pilot's license at age 17. The 20-year-old had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and was working for a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, according to her mother. Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras itsnatfilg/Threads According to the Palm Beach Post , the crash killed Helen Sharp, 40, her husband, Adam Robinson, 45, and their two young children. Sharp's father, 70-year-old Dudley Sharp, confirmed the deaths to the outlet. "It's quite a blow," he told the Palm Beach Post. "We had a daughter, her husband and two grandchildren on the plane." Family members of the seven passengers killed in the Nov. 1 crash released a joint statement on Facebook that also identifies the other three passengers: Anita Maria Cetina, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr. "With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1," the statement said. "Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives. Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return." "Charmi and Rachel were full of joy and adventure," the statement continued. "They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly. Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family. She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion." The families also thanked first responders, investigators and the Palm Beach community for "their care," as well as "everyone who reached out with love." They added: "Our hearts are also with the families of the pilots, who are grieving alongside us." Robinson was a tech entrepreneur from Austin, according to his LinkedIn page. He described himself as the founder and CEO for RB2B and Retention.com. A fellow tech entrepreneur, Jesse Ouellette, shared a tribute on LinkedIn, saying Robinson had helped him when he was building his company. "He became a friend and someone I saw eye to eye with on how to build software companies," said Ouellette. "He could disagree with you about almost anything, and somehow you'd walk away liking him even more." Robinson last posted on LinkedIn on the day of his death, promoting a debate he and Ouellette had scheduled for Nov. 3. Sharp was a sculptural ceramic artist, according to her Instagram account . A tribute posted on her page said she founded a PR company, Influential PR. The pair, according to the same post, met while Sharp was living abroad in Buenos Aires, Argentina. What we know The aircraft crashed in a residential area in Greenacres. Anadolu via Getty Images The Learjet 60 took off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. FAA records list the owner as a Delaware corporation. The National Weather Service had a flood watch in effect for the crash area, Palm Beach County, through Nov. 2, with rain expected on and off across South Florida. In air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC, someone in the cockpit said they were "managing the ice" but faced "moderate" turbulence and were seeking "better rides." The Associated Press reported the crew also asked to climb. Less than a minute later, the person said "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was suddenly descending at 10,000 feet per minute. Seconds later, the person declared an emergency, with the descent rate reaching 20,000 feet per minute. Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: "We're going to crash into the ground," before reporting the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the plane began to bank. Flightradar24 data showed the vertical descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute. The last words heard from the cockpit were "we're out of time." Driver Aki Kuusisto's dashcam footage captured the moment the jet hit the ground. "I heard a whistling noise, a big bang, and I saw a fireball," he told CBS News . "It felt like it was right next to us... you could feel it in the car." The jet is reported to have descended at a peak of 32,000 feet per minute. Anadolu via Getty Images Accuweather reported that thunderstorms in the area produced heavy rainfall and lightning. AP reports that the pilots were warned by controllers about the looming storms as they crossed into Florida and the FAA published an official warning about the weather prior to the plane's departure on Nov. 1. According to AccuWeather, the tops of some of the storm clouds reached up to 45,000 feet, making it difficult for planes to fly over. The plane may not have been able to detect the updrafts that can intensify precipitation, as AccuWeather's Dan DePodwin said that the weather radars on planes have limitations. Chapman said that the investigators are yet to determine what the weather conditions were at 35,000 feet, the altitude the plane was flying at when problems were first reported by the copilot. He added that the investigators hope to recover the cockpit voice recorder. 'A cataclysmic plane crash' Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis told reporters during a Nov. 1 briefing that there was "a lot of debris" that was strewn over a "pretty significant distance." "It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis said. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road." Transportation Secretary Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" and said the FAA and Department of Transportation would be investigating the incident. Anthony Blackmon, who lives around 500 feet from the site of the crash, told NBC Miami that debris from the crash struck his home. "Debris was everywhere," he said. "Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire. I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today." Adam Itayem told WPTV , "It sounded like a loud boom. I thought it was thunder," adding, "I saw a big crater in the ground and water coming out of the crater and a big fire too." "I heard and felt the boom," Andrew Mannino told CNN , saying he saw a "large black cloud immerse in the air," adding, "The power immediately went out and is still out." Around 600 people were evacuated by Palm Beach County authorities while federal officials investigate the crash. "We're waiting for someone to give us answers about what we're going to do, because they're not even letting us into the community to get our clothes," local resident Jesus Solorzano told WPTV.
